cls: Antiretroviral - HIV-1 protease inhibitor (used chiefly as a pharmacokinetic enhancer/booster)
quick: HIV (rare full dose): 600 mg orally twice daily with meals after titration; far more often used at 100-200 mg as a CYP3A4 booster of another protease inhibitor
Take WITH meals to improve tolerability and exposure; swallow tablets whole
Used in pregnancy when indicated; part of recommended boosted ARV regimens
Breastfeeding not recommended in HIV-positive mothers (transmission risk)
No dose adjustment; not removed by dialysis
Caution; avoid/closely monitor in severe hepatic impairment
Avoid excessive alcohol; oral-solution formulation can react with disulfiram/metronidazole
Lipids, glucose, LFTs, and an exhaustive review of all co-medications for CYP3A interactions
summary: Ritonavir is an HIV-1 protease inhibitor now used almost entirely at low dose as a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor to 'boost' the plasma levels and prolong the action of other protease inhibitors (e.g., lopinavir, atazanavir, darunavir). Because it strongly inhibits CYP3A4, it has an extensive list of contraindicated and interacting co-medications whose concentrations can rise to dangerous levels.
indications: Treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination with other antiretroviral agents (tablets in adults; oral powder in pediatric patients)
Low-dose pharmacokinetic boosting of other HIV protease inhibitors

dosage.n: Titrate from 300 mg BID, increasing by 100 mg BID every 2-3 days to reduce GI effects

dosage.d: 350-400 mg/m2 twice daily with meals (max 600 mg BID)
dosage.n: Start 250 mg/m2 BID, titrate by 50 mg/m2 every 2-3 days

dosage.d: 100-200 mg once or twice daily (per partner PI label)
dosage.n: Dose/frequency dictated by the co-administered protease inhibitor

admin: Take with meals to improve tolerability and absorption
Swallow tablets whole - do not chew, break, or crush
Oral powder: mix with soft food (apple sauce, vanilla pudding) or liquid; use within 2 hours
Must always be used in combination with other antiretroviral agents
Review the FULL co-medication list before initiation for CYP3A4 interactions
moa: Ritonavir is a peptidomimetic inhibitor of HIV-1 protease, preventing cleavage of the gag-pol polyprotein and producing immature, non-infectious virions. Clinically it is used mainly as a strong mechanism-based inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4 (and P-glycoprotein), which raises and sustains concentrations of co-administered protease inhibitors ('boosting').

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ritonavir (including TEN or Stevens-Johnson syndrome)

Co-administration with CYP3A-dependent drugs where high levels are dangerous: alfuzosin; ranolazine; amiodarone, dronedarone, flecainide, propafenone, quinidine; voriconazole; colchicine (in renal/hepatic impairment); lurasidone, pimozide; ergot derivatives (dihydroergotamine, ergotamine, methylergonovine); cisapride; lovastatin, simvastatin; lomitapide; sildenafil for pulmonary arterial hypertension; triazolam, oral midazolam
Co-administration with potent CYP3A inducers that lower ritonavir levels: apalutamide; St. John's wort
monitor: Complete review of all concomitant medications

preg: Ritonavir-boosted regimens are used in pregnancy when an antiretroviral is indicated; lopinavir/ritonavir and other boosted PIs are part of recommended regimens. Use as part of an appropriate combination under specialist care.
lact: Where breastfeeding is not advised for HIV-positive mothers (e.g., where safe replacement feeding is available), women should not breastfeed because of HIV transmission risk and potential infant exposure.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required for renal impairment. Ritonavir is highly protein-bound and not appreciably removed by hemodialysis.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; transaminase elevations and hepatitis can occur. Avoid or monitor closely in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibition raises levels of many drugs - see contraindicated list (statins, ergots, sedatives, antiarrhythmics, alfuzosin, etc.)
Other protease inhibitors (intended boosting interaction - dose per their labels)
Tacrolimus, cyclosporine, many anticancer and antifungal agents (need adjustment)
moderate: Hormonal contraceptives (reduced estrogen - use additional contraception)
interactions.food: Take with food to improve tolerability and exposure
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol; the oral-solution formulation can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with metronidazole/disulfiram
interactions.diagnostics: May increase triglycerides, cholesterol, glucose, liver enzymes, uric acid, and creatine kinase

emergency: Life-threatening arrhythmia from an interacting drug

monitoring: CBC, HIV viral load and CD4 as part of therapy
counsel: Always take with food and exactly as prescribed; never miss doses (resistance risk)
Tell every prescriber and pharmacist you take ritonavir - it interacts with very many drugs, including some OTC and herbal products
Do not start any new medicine (including St. John's wort) without checking
Report severe rash, yellowing of skin/eyes, severe abdominal pain, or persistent vomiting
Use additional non-hormonal contraception if relevant
pk: Steady-state antiviral/boosting effect within days of dosing
Plasma peak about 2-4 hours after a dose (with food)
Twice-daily dosing for full-dose use; boosting dose per partner drug
Tablets: store at room temperature, do not refrigerate; oral powder/solution per label
pearls: Modern use is almost exclusively as a low-dose CYP3A4 booster rather than as an antiviral in its own right
Its defining hazard is the enormous interaction profile - always screen co-medications
GI upset and paresthesias are reduced by dose titration when full-dose is used
Cobicistat is an alternative pharmacoenhancer without intrinsic antiviral activity
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered with food, unless it is almost time for the next dose - then skip the missed dose. Do not double up. Strict adherence is essential to prevent resistance.
overdose: Human experience is limited; reported effects include paresthesias and, in post-marketing reports, renal failure with eosinophilia. There is no specific antidote. Treatment is supportive (vital signs, airway); activated charcoal or gastric lavage may help remove unabsorbed drug. Dialysis is unlikely to help because the drug is highly protein-bound and extensively metabolized.
